title: Associations of longitudinal BMI percentile classification patterns in early childhood with neighborhood-level social determinants of health.
ehr_evidence: We obtained patient-level EHR data from Nemours Children’s Health - a large, multi-state pediatric health system in the US.
summary: Longitudinal analysis of BMI-percentile trajectories in early childhood using EHR data, identifying distinct trajectory clusters and assessing their associations with neighborhood-level social determinants of health.
key_findings: Five BMI-percentile trajectory clusters were identified in a cohort of 36,910 children: always having obesity (n=429; 1.16%), overweight most of the time (n=15,006; 40.65%), increasing BMI-percentile (n=9,060; 24.54%), decreasing BMI-percentile (n=5,058; 13.70%), and always normal weight (n=7,357; 19.89%).

Children in the obesity, overweight, and increasing BMI-percentile groups were significantly more likely to reside in neighborhoods with higher poverty, unemployment, crowded households, single-parent households, and lower preschool enrollment compared to the decreasing and normal weight groups.
Multinomial logistic regression confirmed significant associations between neighborhood SDOH and cluster membership, with all confidence intervals for odds ratios excluding 1.
captured_features: patient race, ethnicity, and insurance type
patient addresses linked to census tracts
neighborhood-level SDOH variables (poverty, unemployment, crowded households, single-parent households, preschool enrollment, median household income, etc.)
study_design: Longitudinal cohort study with data-driven and algorithmic clustering of BMI trajectories, followed by multinomial logistic regression analysis.
population: Children aged 0-7 years from a multi-state US pediatric health system (Nemours Children's Health), N=36,910
limitations: Linkage to a single census tract using the last available address may not capture residential mobility effects.
Potential selection bias from excluding children with sparse clinical data or those who left the health system.
Regional differences across the five states were not accounted for.
Did not exclude children on weight-affecting medications or with monogenic obesity.
Did not analyze interactions between different SDOH variables.
